title: slice_codepoint_bounded treats Result-returning stdlib calls as infallible — the change cannot compile
detail: gleam/string's to_utf_codepoints/from_utf_codepoints return Result(List(Int), Nil)/Result(String, Nil); piping a Result into list.take and returning a Result where String is declared is a type error, so the fix and every new test fail to compile — the claimed green suites are impossible.
recommended_fix: Handle the Result: case string.to_utf_codepoints(value) { Ok(cps) -> string.from_utf_codepoints(list.take(cps, max)) |> result.unwrap("") Error(_) -> "" }; mirror the unwrap in codepoint_length.

title: Diff contradicts itself on whether payment_terms_acceptance still carries the 64/512 CHECK constraints
evidence:
+//// Note: of the three original 64/512 CHECK sites, only
+//// `cookie_consent_log` and `application.submitted_*` still carry the
+//// constraints (the `payment_terms_acceptance` ones were dropped by
+//// the 2026-05-12 constraint-parity migration). Bounding beyond what a
+//// CHECK demands is harmless; the helpers stay uniform for all callers.

+**Approach:** Replace grapheme-based slicing with **codepoint-bounded** slicing in the two helper functions. The helpers feed `cookie_consent_log`, `payment_terms_acceptance`, and `application.submitted_*` — all share the same 64/512 CHECK idiom, so the fix lands in one focused change in `request_helpers.gleam` and applies to all three callers unchanged.

+// (refcheck rc1-1 deferred fix regression pin; same CHECK idiom as
+// payment_terms_acceptance and application.submitted_*.)
detail: The new source comment says the payment_terms_acceptance CHECKs were dropped by a migration, while the new spec and consent-test comment say payment shares the same 64/512 CHECK idiom. Both claims are in this diff; at least one is false.
recommended_fix: Reconcile before landing: either restore the payment_terms_acceptance CHECK claims in the spec and consent comment, or delete them; confirm which constraints exist post-migration.

title: Comment says XFF is 140 codepoints; the assertion on the same string says 150
evidence:
+  let xff = string.repeat(family_emoji, 20) <> ", 10.0.0.1"
+  // 20 graphemes = 140 codepoints, over the 64-char ip_text CHECK.
+  codepoint_length(xff) |> should.equal(150)
detail: The comment describes the just-built xff as 140 codepoints, but the assertion counts 150 — the 10-codepoint ', 10.0.0.1' suffix the comment omits. The numbers only reconcile if the reader supplies the missing suffix.
recommended_fix: Amend the comment: '20 graphemes = 140 codepoints, plus 10 for ", 10.0.0.1", = 150 total — past the 64-char CHECK.'

title: File header still enumerates only two callers ('both') though this diff adds application.submitted_* to the consumer docs
detail: The edited header comment still names only payment_handler and consent_handler ('both store the values'), while the same diff's client_user_agent doc and the spec add application_handler/submitted_* as a third consumer. Partially-updated comment.
recommended_fix: Add application_handler (application.submitted_*) to the header comment's consumer list and reword 'both' to 'all callers'.

title: GDPR test comment misstates what grapheme slicing would retain for its own 100-grapheme input
evidence:
+/// Multi-codepoint headers: each family-emoji grapheme is 7 codepoints,
+/// so 100 graphemes = 700 characters by Postgres `length()`. Grapheme
+/// slicing (Gleam `string.slice`) would keep 512 graphemes = 3584
+/// characters past the 512 CHECK and 500 the write path; codepoint
+/// slicing must keep the stored value within the CHECK bound.

+// all 700 codepoints (512 graphemes of 7 codepoints = 3584) — well
detail: The pinned input is 100 graphemes (700 codepoints), so old grapheme slicing would keep 700 codepoints, not '512 graphemes = 3584'. The sibling unit-test comment in the same diff states it correctly; the gdpr comment misdescribes the scenario.
recommended_fix: Reword: 'grapheme slicing would keep all 700 codepoints (100 graphemes), past the 512 CHECK'; reserve the 3584 figure for the general worst case.
